entities.name: Skanderbeg
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gjergj Kastrioti, universally known as Skanderbeg, was an Albanian nobleman and military commander who spearheaded a remarkably effective resistance against the expanding Ottoman Empire for over two decades in the mid-15th century (c. 1443–1468). Born into the Kastrioti principality in 1405, Skanderbeg’s strategic brilliance and unwavering resolve made him a pivotal figure in the defense of Christian Europe against Ottoman incursions, effectively delaying their advance into the Italian peninsula and establishing a profound, enduring legacy as Albania's national hero.

After being taken as a hostage by the Ottomans and serving in their military, Skanderbeg defected in 1443 during the Battle of Niš, returning to Albania to reclaim his ancestral lands. He united the Albanian principalities under the League of Lezhë in 1444, an unprecedented coalition that achieved significant victories against vastly superior Ottoman forces, notably at Torvioll (1444), Oronichea (1448), and Albulena (1457). His defense of Krujë, his stronghold, against multiple Ottoman sieges (most notably in 1450, 1466, and 1467) became legendary, demonstrating his mastery of mountain warfare and guerrilla tactics against Sultans Murad II and Mehmed II.

Skanderbeg's sustained resistance had profound consequences, preventing the Ottoman Empire from consolidating its control over the Balkan Peninsula and projecting power further west into Italy for a critical period. His diplomatic efforts forged alliances with the Kingdom of Naples, the Republic of Venice, and the Papacy, drawing wider European attention and support for the anti-Ottoman cause. Although Albania eventually fell to the Ottomans shortly after his death, Skanderbeg's struggle provided a powerful blueprint for national resistance and became a cornerstone of Albanian national identity and historical memory.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Skanderbeg's two-decade resistance against the Ottoman Empire significantly delayed their advance into Western Europe, safeguarding the Italian peninsula for a critical period. His legacy became a foundational element of Albanian national identity and a potent symbol of defiance against overwhelming odds.
